mainTopic: Pledges in קידושין and sales, and when a woman's instructions about the money count as accepting קידושין
overview: This amud opens with the end of רב נחמן's ruling: a man promised a מנה for קידושין but gave only a pledge, so nothing counts. רבא challenges this from a ברייתא that says קידושין with a pledge works. The גמרא answers that the ברייתא means a pledge the man holds from someone who owes him money. It backs this up with רבי יצחק's proof that a creditor really acquires a pledge. A story with רבי אמי applies the same rule to buying a maidservant. Next come a series of ברייתות about a woman who reacts to the קידושין money: she throws it away, tells him to give it to her father, his father or a stranger, or has it put on a rock or given to a dog or a poor person. The גמרא explains which actions show she accepted the money and why each ruling is needed. Two questions, a shared rock and a chasing dog, end in תיקו. The amud closes as a new story about a seller begins, and it continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Neither the money nor the pledge counts
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן finishes his ruling: the man promised a מנה but gave only a pledge, so nothing valid was given for the קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no מנה here, and there is no pledge here.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the end of רב נחמן's ruling about a man who said 'be betrothed to me with a מנה' and then handed the woman a pledge instead of the money. He rules that the קידושין does not take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מנה was promised but never actually handed over. The pledge was only security, not a gift, so it was never meant to become hers. Since she received nothing that truly belongs to her, there is nothing to make the קידושין work.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred dinars
A pledge, an item given as security for money owed
There is not here, meaning it does not count

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the basic rule that a pledge alone, given as security, cannot work as the money of קידושין.

phrases.english: There is no one hundred dinars here –
phrases.notes: He promised her a מנה but only handed her a pledge, so the actual money never reached her.

phrases.english: there is no pledge here.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָנֶה אֵין כָּאן – מַשְׁכּוֹן אֵין כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב נחמן's ruling from the previous section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who promised a מנה and gave only a pledge has not made קידושין, because neither the promised money nor the security counts.

steps.title: רבא challenges from a ברייתא that pledge betrothal works
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes a ברייתא saying that if a man betroths with a pledge, she is betrothed. This seems to contradict רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised an objection to רב נחמן: If he betrothed her with a pledge, she is betrothed!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's ruling with a teaching that says קידושין with a pledge does work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן just said a pledge does not count. The ברייתא says plainly that a pledge does make קידושין. On the surface the two clash directly.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to Rav Naḥman:
If he betrothed her with a pledge, she is betrothed!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that a pledge does not count for קידושין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא explicitly rules that קידושין with a pledge is valid, which seems to contradict רב נחמן.

steps.title: The ברייתא means a pledge taken from someone else
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is about a pledge the man holds from another person's debt, and it follows רבי יצחק.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is talking about a pledge belonging to others, and it follows the view of רבי יצחק.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב נחמן by saying the ברייתא is talking about a different kind of pledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב נחמן's case, the man gave the woman his own item as security, so it was never meant to be hers. In the ברייתא, the man had lent money to someone else and was holding that person's pledge, and he betroths her with it. Following רבי יצחק, a creditor has real ownership rights in such a pledge, so he can give those rights to her.

keyTerms.meaning: Of others, belonging to other people
And in line with the view of רבי

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two pledges. רב נחמן's case is the man's own item given to the woman as security. The ברייתא's case is a borrower's item that the man holds as a creditor.

phrases.english: There, it is with a pledge belonging to others
phrases.notes: He means a pledge the man is holding from someone who owes him money.

phrases.english: and it is in accordance with Rabbi Yitzḥak.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ברייתא is moved to a different kind of pledge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that any pledge, even the man's own item given as security, makes קידושין.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא only means a pledge held from another person's debt, where the creditor owns real rights in it, as רבי יצחק teaches.

steps.title: רבי יצחק: a creditor acquires the pledge
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק proves from a פסוק that a creditor gains ownership in a pledge, because returning it is called צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק says: From where do we know that a creditor acquires a pledge? The פסוק says, 'And it shall be צדקה for you.' If he did not acquire it, why would returning it be צדקה? From here we learn that a creditor acquires a pledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבי יצחק's teaching to explain the answer in step 3. He shows from the תורה that a creditor really owns something in the pledge he holds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה tells a creditor to return a poor borrower's pledge at night and calls this צדקה. You can only give צדקה with something that is yours. So the creditor must have real ownership in the pledge, and that ownership is what the man in the ברייתא gives to the woman.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, the one owed money

steps.whatToRemember: A creditor holding a borrower's pledge has real ownership rights in it, so he can use it for קידושין. A man's own item given only as security cannot be used that way.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבי יצחק's principle, that a creditor acquires a pledge, matters for many questions of lending and ownership, not only קידושין.

phrases.english: As Rabbi Yitzḥak says:
From where do we know that a creditor acquires a pledge –
as it is stated: “And it shall be righteousness to you” –
if he does not acquire it, from where is there righteousness?
phrases.notes: Returning something that was never yours would not be giving anything, so it could not be called צדקה.

phrases.english: From here we learn that a creditor acquires a pledge.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: מִנַּיִן לְבַעַל חוֹב שֶׁקּוֹנֶה מַשְׁכּוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the teaching of רבי יצחק mentioned in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A creditor gains ownership in a pledge he holds, learned from the פסוק that calls returning it צדקה.

steps.title: The case of the maidservant bought with a silver pledge
steps.stepSummary: The sons of רב הונא בר אבין bought a maidservant for coins but left a silver piece as a pledge. Her price went up, and they came to רבי אמי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sons of רב הונא בר אבין bought a certain maidservant for small coins. They did not have the coins with them, so they left a silver piece for her. In the end the maidservant's price went up. They came before רבי אמי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that tests the same pledge question in a sale. This step sets up the facts and brings the question to רבי אמי, whose answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers did not pay the agreed coins. They only left a silver piece as security. When her value rose, the seller wanted out, so the question became whether the pledge had already completed the purchase.

keyTerms.meaning: A piece of silver, a bar of metal

phrases.english: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
bought a certain maidservant for small coins,
they did not have them with them,
so they placed a piece of silver for her.
phrases.notes: The silver was left only as security until they could bring the coins, not as payment.

phrases.english: In the end, the maidservant became more expensive.
They came before Rabbi Ami,

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי רַב הוּנָא בַּר אָבִין זְבוּן הָהִיא אַמְתָּא בִּפְרִיטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a real case similar to רב נחמן's ruling in step 1, this time about a sale.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a pledge left in place of the agreed payment complete the purchase of the maidservant?

steps.title: רבי אמי: neither the coins nor the silver counts
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי rules that no purchase happened: the coins were never paid and the silver was only a pledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: There are no coins here, and there is no silver piece here.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי answers the case, using the same wording as רב נחמן. The sale never took effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The agreed price, the coins, was never handed over. The silver piece was only security, so it did not count as payment. Since nothing valid was paid, the seller may back out.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רב נחמן and רבי אמי teach that a pledge given only as security cannot replace the actual payment, whether for קידושין or for a purchase.

phrases.english: He said to them: There are no coins here,
there is no piece of silver here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: פְּרִיטֵי אֵין כָּאן, נְסָכָא אֵין כָּאן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The purchase did not happen, because the coins were not paid and the silver was only a pledge.

steps.title: She threw the money into the sea: not betrothed
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if she took the מנה and threw it into the sea, the fire, or anywhere it is lost, she is not betrothed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If he said, 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,' and she took it and threw it into the sea, or into the fire, or anywhere it gets lost, she is not betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about a woman who destroys the קידושין money right after getting it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By destroying the money, she shows she does not accept it as קידושין. So even though it touched her hand, the קידושין does not take effect.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that gets lost or destroyed

phrases.english: The Sages taught: “Be betrothed to me with one hundred dinars,”
and she took it and threw it into the sea or into the fire
or into anything that destroys –
she is not betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the pledge discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If a woman destroys the קידושין money right after taking it, she is not betrothed.

steps.title: Would throwing it back at him really be betrothal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers from the ברייתא that throwing the money back at him would be קידושין, and is surprised, since that clearly means 'take it, I don't want it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: This implies that if she threw it in front of him, it is קידושין? But she is saying to him: Take it, I don't want it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads an implication out of the ברייתא and challenges it. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא only says destroying the money cancels the קידושין. That suggests throwing it back to him would still count. But throwing it back is an even clearer refusal, so the inference seems impossible.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא never says that throwing it back is קידושין. The גמרא is drawing this from what the ברייתא leaves out, and it questions that inference.

phrases.english: But if she threw them before him –
it would be a betrothal?
But she is saying to him:
Take it, I do not want it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges what the ברייתא in step 7 seems to imply.
steps.kashyaTarget: What the ברייתא seems to imply: that throwing the money back at him would be valid קידושין
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Throwing the money back at him clearly shows she refuses it, so it could not possibly count as accepting קידושין.

steps.title: The ברייתא is speaking in a 'no need to say' style
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא never meant that throwing the money back at him works. Throwing it at him is obviously not קידושין. The ברייתא teaches the bigger חידוש: even throwing it into the sea or fire is not קידושין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא is saying 'it goes without saying.' It goes without saying that if she threw the money in front of him, it is not קידושין. But if she threw it into the sea or the fire, you might say: since she is now responsible to pay him back, she must have betrothed herself. And why did she destroy it? She wanted to test this man to see if he has a hot temper or not. So the ברייתא teaches us that even then, it is not קידושין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 8. The ברייתא picked the sea and fire cases because they are the harder ones, not because throwing it at him would work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing the money back at him clearly means 'I don't want it,' so it needs no teaching. Destroying the money could be misread: she becomes liable to repay it, so maybe she kept it as קידושין and only wanted to test his temper. The ברייתא rules that even this is not קידושין.

keyTerms.meaning: It goes without saying; a style that teaches the harder case and assumes the easier one
She is obligated or liable to pay

steps.whatToRemember: A ברייתא often mentions the hardest case and leaves the obvious one unsaid. Here, the hardest case is throwing the money into the sea or fire, and the obvious case is throwing it back at him.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the ברייתא as saying that throwing the money back at him is קידושין. The 'לא מיבעיא' style means that case is even more obviously not קידושין.

phrases.english: It is saying 'it goes without saying':
phrases.notes: The answer is that the ברייתא mentions the harder case and leaves the easy case unspoken.

phrases.english: It goes without saying that if she threw them in front of him
it is not קידושין,
but if she threw it into the sea or into the fire,
I might say: since she is liable to repay them,
she has betrothed herself,
and the reason she acted this way
is that she thought: I will test this man
to see if he is hot-tempered or not;
so it teaches us (that it is not קידושין).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's wording suggests that throwing the money back at him would be קידושין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Throwing it at him is obviously not קידושין. The ברייתא tells us that even destroying it, which makes her liable to repay, is not קידושין.

steps.title: A ברייתא about giving the money to her father or his father
steps.stepSummary: If she tells him to give the money to her father or to his father, she is not betrothed. If she adds 'on condition that he accepts it for me,' she is betrothed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: A man says, 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה.' She answers, 'Give it to my father' or 'to your father.' She is not betrothed. If she says, 'on condition that he accepts it for me,' she is betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It deals with a woman who tells the man to hand the קידושין money to someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply sending the money to another person does not count as her receiving it. If she makes that person her receiver ('accept it for me'), then his receiving counts as hers, and the קידושין works.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינרים

phrases.english: The רבנן taught:
If he said, 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,'
and she said, 'Give them to my father' or 'to your father,'
phrases.notes: The 'and' here means 'or': two separate cases, her father or his father.

phrases.english: she is not betrothed.
If she said, 'on condition that he accepts them for me,'
she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: handing the money to a third party.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Telling him to give the money to someone else is not קידושין, unless that person accepts it on her behalf.

steps.title: Why the ברייתא mentions both fathers
steps.stepSummary: 'My father' shows how strong the first ruling is. 'Your father' shows how strong the second ruling is.
steps.simpleTranslation: It mentioned 'my father' to show the strength of the first part. It mentioned 'your father' to show the strength of the last part.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ברייתא needed both examples, her father and his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First part: even when the money goes to her own father, whom she surely wants to benefit, she is still not betrothed. Last part: when she names someone to accept it for her, the קידושין works even if that person is the man's own father.

keyTerms.meaning: To show you the strength of (how far a ruling goes)
The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching

phrases.english: It taught 'my father'
to show you the strength of the first part;
phrases.notes: Even when the money goes to her own father, she is not betrothed.

phrases.english: it taught 'your father'
to show you the strength of the last part.
phrases.notes: Even his own father can accept for her, and she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the wording of the ברייתא in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each father is mentioned to show the furthest reach of one part of the ruling.

steps.title: The same rule with 'so-and-so'
steps.stepSummary: A similar ruling: if she says 'give it to so-and-so,' she is not betrothed. If she says 'on condition that he accepts it for me,' she is betrothed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,' and she said, 'Give them to so-and-so,' she is not betrothed. If she said, 'on condition that he accepts them for me,' she is betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling that looks almost the same as the last one. This time the other person is any person, not a father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is the same as before. Sending the money elsewhere does not count, but naming a receiver for her does. Because it looks like a repeat, the גמרא will next explain why it is needed.

phrases.english: If he said, 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,'
and she said, 'Give them to so-and-so,'
she is not betrothed.
If she said, 'on condition that he accepts them for me,'
she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel ruling to step 10, with any third person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Money given to any third person is not קידושין unless that person accepts it for her.

steps.title: Both rulings are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says both rulings are necessary, and the explanation comes next.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is necessary (to teach both).
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא says the two similar rulings are both needed, and it will explain why in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an unspoken question: why repeat a rule we already know? 'וצריכא' says each ruling teaches something the other could not. The details come right after this.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary (both teachings are needed)

phrases.english: And it is necessary,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the unspoken question of why step 12 repeats step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each teaching is needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second ruling seems to repeat the first.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both are needed. Steps 14 and 15 give the reasons.

steps.title: Why the 'father' case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: If we had only the 'my father / your father' ruling, we might think the condition 'he accepts it for me' works only with close relatives she trusts, and not with a stranger.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we had only been taught 'my father and your father,' we would say: only there, when she adds 'on condition that they accept it for me,' is it קידושין, because she trusts them to act as her messengers. But with a stranger, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first half of its reason why both rulings are needed. It shows what mistake we would make if we only had the 'father' case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a father, she can rely on him to really act as her messenger and accept the money for her. A stranger might not do her errand, so we might think the condition fails with him. The 'so-and-so' ruling teaches that the condition works even with a stranger.

keyTerms.meaning: It taught us / it let us hear
On condition that they accept it for me
Being a messenger / doing an errand for someone

phrases.english: For if it had taught us only 'my father' and 'your father,'
it is there that when she said
'on condition that they accept it for me,' it is a valid betrothal,
because she relies on them,
phrases.notes: Some versions spell 'on them' a little differently. The letter in square brackets is the corrected spelling.

phrases.english: she thinks: they will do my errand for me.
But with so-and-so, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the explanation of the צריכא that was announced in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each ruling teaches something the other cannot
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The condition 'he accepts it for me' works only with a close relative she trusts.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'so-and-so' ruling shows the condition works even with a stranger.

steps.title: Why the 'stranger' case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: If we had only the 'so-and-so' ruling, we might think that with a father she is betrothed, because she may have accepted the money and given it to him as a gift. So both rulings are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if we had only been taught 'so-and-so,' we would say: only here, when she says 'give it to so-and-so,' is it not קידושין, because she is not close to him and would not give him a gift. But with my father or your father, whom she is close to, I might say she accepted the money and gave it to them as a gift. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second half of its reason and finishes with 'צריכא,' meaning both rulings are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman would not give a gift to a stranger, so 'give it to so-and-so' clearly does not show she accepted the money. With a close relative, we might think she accepted the קידושין and then passed the money on as a gift. The 'father' ruling teaches that even then she is not betrothed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary (both rulings are needed)

steps.whatToRemember: Each ruling blocks a different mistake. 'Father' teaches that even with someone close, a plain 'give it to him' is not קידושין. 'So-and-so' teaches that the condition 'he accepts it for me' works even with a stranger.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only so-and-so,
it is here that when she said 'give it to so-and-so'
it is not a betrothal,
because she does not feel close to him
to give it to him as a gift.
But 'my father' and 'your father,'
whom she feels close to,
I might say she gave it to them as a gift,
so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the צריכא explanation that began in step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With a close relative, she may have accepted the money and given it as a gift, so she would be betrothed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with a close relative, 'give it to him' alone is not קידושין.

steps.title: Placing the money on a rock
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: if she tells him to put the money on a rock, she is not betrothed. If the rock is hers, she is betrothed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: He says 'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,' and she says 'Put it on a rock.' She is not betrothed. But if the rock was hers, she is betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a woman who tells the man to put the money somewhere instead of handing it to her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Putting the money on any rock does not give it to her, so nothing has happened. But if the rock belongs to her, the money ends up on her own property. That counts as if she received it.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינרים
Here: a rock (it can also mean a coin)

steps.confusionAlert: Here סלע means a rock, not the coin called a סלע.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
'Be betrothed to me with a מנה,'
and she said 'Put them on a rock.'
She is not betrothed.
And if the rock was hers, she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ברייתא with a related case: telling him to put the money somewhere instead of in her hand.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Putting the money on an ownerless or someone else's rock is not קידושין. Putting it on her own rock is.

steps.title: What if the rock belongs to both of them?
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי asks about a rock that the man and woman own together.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי asked: If the rock belongs to both of them, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב ביבי asks about a case in between the two rulings of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא told us about a rock that is not hers and a rock that is hers. A shared rock is partly hers and partly his. Does it count as her property or not?

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (a real question of law)

phrases.english: רב ביבי asked:
A rock belonging to both of them, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a middle case between the two rulings of the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a jointly owned rock count as her property for קידושין?

steps.title: The question stays unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says תיקו: the question of the shared rock is left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds no answer to רב ביבי's question and leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיקו means the question stands without a decision. So the case of a shared rock stays a doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand: the question stays unanswered

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends רב ביבי's question without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether a shared rock works for קידושין remains a doubt.

steps.title: Giving the loaf to a dog
steps.stepSummary: A parallel case: if she tells him to give the bread to a dog, she is not betrothed. If it is her dog, she is betrothed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He says 'Be betrothed to me with a loaf of bread,' and she says 'Give it to a dog.' She is not betrothed. But if the dog was hers, she is betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a similar case, this time a loaf of bread and a dog.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeding some random dog gives her nothing, so there is no קידושין. Feeding her own dog benefits her, because it feeds her animal. So she is betrothed.

phrases.english: 'Be betrothed to me with a loaf,'
and she said 'Give it to a dog.'
She is not betrothed.
And if the dog was hers, she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case to the rock, built the same way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Giving the loaf to someone else's dog is not קידושין. Giving it to her own dog is.

steps.title: What if the dog was chasing her?
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי asks about a dog that was running after her, when she tells him to give it the bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי asked: If a dog was running after her, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי asks a new question about the dog case. The next step lays out both sides, and the question ends unresolved with תיקו in step 22.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dog is not hers, but feeding it would help her escape from it. The question is whether that help counts as a benefit she received, which would make her betrothed.

phrases.english: רב מרי asked:
A dog running after her, what is the law?
phrases.notes: She tells him to give the bread to that dog, so it will leave her alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about a middle case in the dog ruling, just as רב ביבי asked about the rock.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does being saved from a dog that is not hers count as receiving value for קידושין?

steps.title: The two sides of the question about the chasing dog
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי lays out both sides: does being saved from the dog count as a benefit that makes her betrothed, or can she say he was already obligated by Torah law to save her?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do we say that because she gets the benefit of being saved from the dog, she commits herself and gives herself to him in קידושין? Or maybe she can say to him: 'By Torah law you were obligated to save me anyway.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is spelling out the two possible ways to look at רב מרי's question about the dog that was chasing her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: she really did gain something, since she was rescued, so that הנאה can work as קידושין. Side two: he did nothing extra for her, because the Torah already required him to rescue her. So she never received a real gift from him.

keyTerms.meaning: She saves herself; she is rescued
She commits and transfers (herself in קידושין)
Or perhaps; it introduces the other side of a question

phrases.aramaic: בְּהָהוּא הֲנָאָה דְּקָא מַצְּלָה נַפְשָׁהּ מִינֵּיהּ
phrases.english: Through that benefit, that she is saving herself from it (the dog),
does she commit herself and transfer herself to him?
Or perhaps she can say to him:
"By Torah law you are obligated to rescue me"?
phrases.notes: This is the מצוה not to stand by while someone is in danger (ויקרא 19:16). Literally it says "to rescue us".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רב מרי's question from step 20 by laying out both possible answers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the benefit of being rescued from a dog count as קידושין, even though he was obligated by Torah law to rescue her?

steps.title: The chasing dog question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רב מרי's question unanswered: תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand. The question is not resolved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion about the chasing dog without deciding which side is right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like רב ביבי's question about the shared rock, this question gets no answer. Both sides stay possible, so we do not know if she is betrothed.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question stays unresolved
A doubt; the status that results when a question is left unresolved

phrases.english: Let it stand (unresolved).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question raised in steps 20-21.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We do not know whether the benefit of being saved from a chasing dog works as קידושין.

steps.title: Giving the bread to a poor person does not make her betrothed
steps.stepSummary: If he offers קידושין with a loaf and she says to give it to a poor person, she is not betrothed, even if that poor person depends on her.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says, 'Be betrothed to me with a loaf,' and she says, 'Give it to a poor person,' she is not betrothed. This is true even if the poor person is one she regularly supports.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case in the same pattern as the rock and the dog. Here the bread goes to a poor person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think that giving to a poor person she usually feeds saves her money, so it counts as her benefit. The ruling says no: she is still not betrothed. The next step explains why.

keyTerms.meaning: Who depends on her; whom she regularly supports

phrases.english: "Be betrothed to me with a loaf"
"Give it to a poor person"
she is not betrothed,
even a poor person who depends on her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case that follows the same pattern as the rock (step 16) and the dog (step 19).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Telling him to give the קידושין bread to a poor person, even one who depends on her, does not make her betrothed.

steps.title: Why the poor person case fails: both are equally obligated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason. She can say to him that he has the same duty to give to the poor that she has.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? She can say to him: 'Just as I am obligated to support him, so are you obligated to support him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the poor person case fails and answers it right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving to a poor person is a מצוה that falls on everyone, including the man. So when he gives, he is doing his own duty and not giving her a gift. The reasoning is like the 'you had to save me anyway' side of the dog question, but here the גמרא is sure of it.
steps.whatToRemember: A benefit only works for קידושין if he is giving her something real. If he is just doing a duty he already has, like giving צדקה, it does not count.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
She can say to him:
Just as I am obligated toward him,
so too you are obligated toward him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the ruling in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is she not betrothed when the bread goes to a poor person she supports?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He has the same duty of צדקה toward the poor person as she does, so his giving is not a gift to her.

steps.title: A new story begins: a man who was selling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story about a certain man who was selling something.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain man who was selling...
steps.whatsHappening: This is only the opening line of a new story. The גמרא is setting up the next case, and the story continues in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase הָהוּא גַּבְרָא tells us a real event is about to be told. We do not yet know what he was selling or what question comes up.

keyTerms.meaning: A certain man; it opens a story
Who was (in the middle of doing something)

phrases.english: There was a certain man
who was selling

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the bread cases to a new story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This line sets up a story that continues in the next part.
